[{"order":1,"type":"heading","text":"Transformer Architecture: Encoder-Decoder and Positional Encoding"},{"order":2,"type":"paragraph","text":"Introduced in the seminal paper 'Attention Is All You Need' (Vaswani et al., 2017), the Transformer architecture revolutionized natural language processing and deep learning. By completely replacing recurrence and convolution with self-attention mechanisms, Transformers achieved state-of-the-art results while drastically improving training parallelism."},{"order":3,"type":"subheading","text":"1. The Need for Positional Encoding"},{"order":4,"type":"paragraph","text":"Unlike Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs), which process tokens sequentially step-by-step, the Transformer architecture processes all tokens in a sequence concurrently. While this enables massive parallelization on GPU hardware, it creates a fundamental challenge: the network inherently lacks any notion of sequence order or token positions."},{"order":5,"type":"paragraph","text":"To inject positional information into the model without altering vector dimensions, Positional Encodings (PE) are added directly to the input embeddings before feeding them into the first encoder or decoder block."},{"order":6,"type":"subheading","text":"Mathematical Formulation of Positional Encoding"},{"order":7,"type":"paragraph","text":"The original Transformer uses fixed sinusoidal functions of varying frequencies to compute positional encodings for each token index:"},{"order":8,"type":"bullet_point","text":"PE(pos, 2i) = sin(pos / 10000^(2i / d_model))"},{"order":9,"type":"bullet_point","text":"PE(pos, 2i+1) = cos(pos / 10000^(2i / d_model))"},{"order":10,"type":"paragraph","text":"In these equations, 'pos' refers to the position of the token in the sequence, 'i' corresponds to the dimension index (ranging from 0 to d_model/2), and 'd_model' is the total embedding dimensionality. This continuous geometric progression allows the model to easily learn relative positions, as PE(pos + k) can be represented as a linear function of PE(pos)."},{"order":11,"type":"subheading","text":"PyTorch Implementation of Positional Encoding"},{"order":12,"type":"code","text":"import torch
import torch.nn as nn
import math

class PositionalEncoding(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, d_model: int, max_len: int = 5000):
        super().__init__()
        # Create a tensor of shape (max_len, d_model) initialized with zeros
        pe = torch.zeros(max_len, d_model)
        
        # Tensor of positions [0, 1, 2, ..., max_len-1]
        position = torch.arange(0, max_len, dtype=torch.float).unsqueeze(1)
        
        # Compute the division term in log-space for numerical stability
        div_term = torch.exp(torch.arange(0, d_model, 2).float() * (-math.log(10000.0) / d_model))
        
        # Apply sine to even indices; cosine to odd indices
        pe[:, 0::2] = torch.sin(position * div_term)
        pe[:, 1::2] = torch.cos(position * div_term)
        
        # Add a batch dimension: (1, max_len, d_model)
        pe = pe.unsqueeze(0)
        
        # Register as a persistent buffer (not a trainable parameter)
        self.register_buffer("pe", pe)

    def forward(self, x: torch.Tensor) -> torch.Tensor:
        # x shape: [batch_size, seq_len, d_model]
        x = x + self.pe[:, :x.size(1)]
        return x"},{"order":13,"type":"subheading","text":"2. High-Level Encoder-Decoder Architecture"},{"order":14,"type":"paragraph","text":"The classic Transformer architecture consists of two primary operational modules: an Encoder stack on the left and a Decoder stack on the right. Both components utilize residual connections around each constituent sub-layer, followed by Layer Normalization."},{"order":15,"type":"subheading","text":"The Encoder Stack"},{"order":16,"type":"paragraph","text":"The Encoder processes input token sequences into rich contextual representations. It consists of N identical stacked layers (typically N=6 or N=12). Each layer comprises two core sub-layers:"},{"order":17,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Multi-Head Self-Attention: Allows tokens to dynamically attend to contextual dependencies across the entire input sequence."},{"order":18,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Position-wise Feed-Forward Network (FFN): Applies two fully-connected linear transformations with an activation function (e.g., ReLU or GELU) in between, independently at each sequence position."},{"order":19,"type":"subheading","text":"The Decoder Stack"},{"order":20,"type":"paragraph","text":"The Decoder is responsible for generating the target sequence autoregressively. Each layer in the Decoder stack contains three sub-layers:"},{"order":21,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Masked Multi-Head Self-Attention: Ensures that token predictions at step 't' depend only on known outputs from steps prior to 't' by applying a upper-triangular causal mask."},{"order":22,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Encoder-Decoder Attention (Cross-Attention): Queries (Q) are derived from the previous decoder sub-layer, whereas Keys (K) and Values (V) originate from the final output representations of the Encoder stack."},{"order":23,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Position-wise Feed-Forward Network: Identical in structure to the encoder feed-forward network."},{"order":24,"type":"subheading","text":"3. End-to-End Information Flow"},{"order":25,"type":"paragraph","text":"During training, source tokens are transformed into input embeddings, combined with positional encodings, and processed through the Encoder stack to yield key-value representations. Simultaneously, shifted target tokens are fed to the Decoder with causal masking enabled. The final Decoder output passes through a linear projection layer and a Softmax function to produce predicted probabilities over the vocabulary."}]
